                                      All of the neutralisation reactions progress relative quickly. De-
                                      struction of all chlorine can be confirmed by adding 3% hydro-
                                      gen peroxide to a waste sample. If the sample fizzes, then free
                                      chlorine remains in the waste. By-product salts may also accu-
                                      mulate in the form of sulphates and chlorides that can cause
                                      corrosion problems. Also, there may be a notable shift in the
                                      pH valve results and control of the reactions is relatively com-
                                      plicated since the end point of the neutralisation cannot be
                                      measured with simple instrumentation methods.

                      Note:           These reactions may produce heat, this must be taken into ac-
                                      count!

                      • Neutralisation Chemicals
                        Neutralisation reactions can be controlled using available chlorine ti-
                        trations or oxidation/reduction potential (ORP) measurements. It is im-
                        portant to have adequate equipment and/or process systems and
                        operating procedures to handle neutralisation reactions and to always
                        read and follow information contained in the MSDS for each of the neu-
                        tralisation chemicals including proper personal protective equipment.
                             • Hydrogen Peroxide
                               One of the chemicals suitable for the reduction of hypochlorite ion
                               available chlorine in sodium hypochlorite is hydrogen peroxide
                               (H2O2), less than 35% concentration. The chemical reaction is as
                               follows:

                                  NaOCl + H2O2 = NaCl + H2O + O2

                                  The sodium hypochlorite reacts spontaneously with the hydrogen
                                  peroxide and the resulting salt solution is adjusted for pH before
                                  discharge. The oxygen is vented to atmosphere at a safe point of
                                  discharge. An advantage of using hydrogen peroxide is the only
                                  end products are salt and water.


                                  This reaction can easily be done on a batch basis in one tank with
                                  neutralisation of the bleach first and pH adjustment second. On a
                                  continuous system, the solution is neutralised in a reactor vessel

                                  in the first step and then the pH is adjusted downstream in a sec-
                                  ond reactor. The hydrogen peroxide is added in the first tank and
                                  acid is added to the second with the appropriate PORP and pH
                                  control systems.
                             • Sulphur Dioxide
                             • Sulphur dioxide (SO2) is a corrosive gas and a safety program
                               must be developed. The use of sulphur dioxide to neutralise sodi-
                               um hypochlorite may result in release of gaseous chlorine if the pH
                               is allowed to drop too low; a release of gaseous SO2 may also re-
                               sult. Therefore, it is important to control the pH until all hypochlorite
                               ions is destroyed and to be sure sulphur dioxide can no longer be
                               released.
                             • Sulphur dioxide can be used for the reduction of available chlorine
                               in sodium hypochlorite. The chemical reaction is as follows:
                             • NaOCl + 2NaOH + SO2 = Na2SO4 + NaCl + H2O
                             • Sodium Sulphite
                               Sodium sulphite can be used for reduction of available chlorine in
                               sodium hypochlorite. The chemical reaction is as follows:
                             • NaOCl + Na2SO3 = NaCl + Na2SO4
                             • Small spills of standing sodium hypochlorite have been neutralised
                               using sodium sulphite applied to the spill. This method has been
                               used to neutralise spills on roadways, bar ditches, and in parking
                               lots. This method should be covered with the local environmental
                               regulating agency in the review of the Spill Control Plan.
                             • Sodium Bisulphite
                               Sodium bisulphite can be used for reduction of available chlorine
                               in sodium hypochlorite. The chemical reaction is as follows:

                                  NaOCl + NaHSO3 = NaCl + NaHSO4

                                  Sodium bisulphite has been used to neutralise the available chlo-
                                  rine in bleach solutions. This reaction can be more vigorous than
                                  the other neutralising chemicals listed. Appropriate personal pro-
                                  tective equipment (PPE) and engineering controls should be used.
                                  This method should be covered with the local environmental regu-
                                  lating agency in the review of the Spill Control Plan.

1.8.9.4.3 Bulk Handling of Sodium Hypochlorite Solution
                      Bulk Tank Trailers (Tankers)
                      Bulk sodium hypochlorite solutions are typically delivered in tank trailers
                      of various capacities. Weight restrictions limit the capacity of these trail-
                      ers in some countries to a maximum of around 20,000 litres or less.

                      • Materials of Construction/Liners
                        Tankers used in the transportation of this product are normally con-
                        structed of FRP or lined carbon steel, as hypochlorite solutions are not
                        compatible with the carbon or stainless steel composites. Examples of
                        lining materials used include rubber such as chlorobutyl, and selected
                        fluoropolymers. Many factors should be considered when selecting a
                        material for these tanks; such as volume to be transported, strength of
                        solution, climate and the expected life of the material.
                      • Pressure Vessels
                        Most tanks in this service are pressure vessels equipped with rupture
                        protection and an eduction tube, therefore, product is usually unloaded
                        by pressuring the tanks, typically with air, though other gases can be
                        used. This process forces the product through the eduction tube, the
                        external piping, the unloading hose, the ridge storage tank piping, and
                        finally into the storage tank itself. Many precautions, which should be
                        identified in each location’s Standard Operating Procedures, must be
                        observed before, during, and after the unloading process to ensure the
                        safe operation of this equipment.
                      • Tank Requirements
                        Tankers used in hazardous material service bust be built to specifica-
                        tions, tested, and marked according to the appropriate regulations.
                        Tankers shall be properly equipped with the appropriate accessory
                        equipment (i.e. manway, rupture disks, vents, etc.) and inspected an-
                        nually. Tankers can only repaired by a certified facility.
                      • Equipment in Mixed Service
                        It is generally not recommended to ship other liquids in a bulk tank trail-
                        er that has been used in sodium hypochlorite service. If this is done, it
                        is the shippers responsibility to ensure that the products are compati-
                        ble and/or that the trailer is completely cleaned between services to
                        prevent any contamination of products or adverse chemical reactions.
                        It is important to confirm the effectiveness of any trailer washing sys-
                        tem used.

                      Placarding
                      Placarding requirements for bulk loads of hypochlorite solutions vary
                      slightly depending on the style and size of the tank, and how the tank is
                      transported. For normal tank trailers placarding consist of the corrosive,
                      in association with the appropriate identification number which must be
                      affixed to both sides and both ends of the transport vehicle.

                      Bulk Loading/Unloading
                      Sodium hypochlorite solutions are typically transported in bulk tank trail-
                      ers with a capacity of around 20,000 litres.

                      • General Precautions
                        Only workers who have received proper instruction in the handling of
                        hazardous materials should perform all loading/unloading operations.
                        They should be fully aware of the product’s properties, its potential
                        hazards, and proper procedures, including all necessary safety pre-
                        caution.

                          A worker must be present throughout the entire loading/unloading op-
                          eration. These activities should only be undertaken during daylight
                          hours or when adequate artificial lighting is available.

                          Proper procedures will minimize potential emissions of fumes or liquid.
                          However, with accidental releases possible, workers should exercise
                          extreme care and wear proper safety equipment. A hazard analysis for
                          this operation should be used to determine what safety equipment is
                          needed at your site for the operations being performed. This could in-
                          clude, but is not limited to chemical splash goggles, rubber gloves, rub-
                          ber boots, chemically resistant protective clothing and a hard hat. The
                          hazard analysis for this operation will determine if additional safety
                          equipment is needed at your site.

                          A safety shower and eye wash foundation (or other source of clean,
                          running water) should be readily accessible in case of emergency. The
                          operation of these critical safety devices should be checked on a reg-
                          ular basis and before starting any work in the area. Suitable spill con-
                          trol equipment should also be available to isolate and contain any
                          potential leaks. Loading/unloading personnel should be trained to han-
                          dle spills of any size.

                      • Standard Operating Procedures
                        Companies involved with the production and handling of hazardous
                        materials should have a program where all standard operating proce-
                        dures for their processes should be written in simple and understand-
                        able language and step by step format, reviewed for safety and
                        environmental issues and validated for accuracy. This program should
                        be developed to cover topics such as details of tasks performed, pro-
                        cedures used to ensure compatible materials of construction, replace-
                        ment materials, new materials, etc., used in the process, equipment
                        knowledge, types and frequency of instrument readings and samples
                        to be taken. Other pertinent information includes safety precautions,
                        critical parameters, safe operating limits, human factors, (i.e. commu-
                        nication issues, operator/equipment interfaces) and adequate measur-
                        ing devices. A preventive maintenance program should also be
                        incorporated into these procedures to avoid a failure in a process sys-
                        tem. The goals of the program should be to educate the new employ-
                        ee, update the existing employees, and maintain the integrity of the
                        production system thereby, eliminating most problems before they oc-
                        cur.



1.8.9.5    Sulphuric Acid
                      Sulphuric acid is used in the Chlorine Plant as a drying medium for the
                      wet chlorine gas.

                      It is delivered from Battery Limit as a 98% w/w solution and is stored in a
                      storage tank within the Chlorine Plant B.L.

                      During the drying process the sulphuric acid picks up the moisture from
                      the wet chlorine gas and is being diluted to 78% w/w in the process.

                      The 78% sulphuric acid is stored in a separate storage tank from where
                      it is transferred to B.L.

                      Please refer to Units 210 / 211 / 212, chapter 8, Chlorine Drying.

                      Chemical and Physical Properties

                      Sulphuric acid is made by combining sulphur trioxide and water:

                             SO2 + H2O = H2SO4

                      Sulphuric acid is a clear to slightly cloudy liquid. It is highly corrosive and
                      attacks metals with the evolution of hydrogen gas, particularly at concen-
                      trations below 80%.

                      Strengths - The following strengths are representative of what is commer-
                      cially available:

1.8.9.5.1 Safe Handling
                      Although sulphuric acid is a highly corrosive liquid, if can be handled safe-
                      ly by observing certain basic precautions. These precautions are dis-
                      cussed here:

                      The greatest danger in the handling of sulphuric acid is getting it in con-
                      tact with any part of the body. Workmen, in addition to being fully instruct-
                      ed on proper procedures to be followed, must be provided with protective
                      clothing such as rubber gloves, hat, coat, pants and boots, as the situa-
                      tion may require.

                      (Regarding rubber boots, pantlegs must always be outside the bootleg,
                      never tucked in.) Tight-fitting goggles and face shield must be provided.

                      Safety showers should be located strategically throughout the working ar-
                      ea, as well as eyewash fountains.

                      Highly flammable hydrogen gas is formed when sulphuric acid is stored
                      in steel storage tanks or drums. Smoking, cutting or welding must not,
                      therefore, be allowed in the immediate vicinity of the tank. Only spark-
                      proof tools should be used. If alterations to the system require the use of
                      fire, then the tank must be emptied and purged completely of hydrogen
                      gas.

                      Sulphuric acid tanks, drums and pipelines must be properly vented to pre-
                      vent the buildup of hydrogen pressure, possibly leading to failure of the
                      equipment.

                      In handling sulphuric acid, any leak occurring in pipe lines or equipment
                      should be considered as an acid leak and treated accordingly with ex-
                      treme caution until proven to be otherwise. A contaminated area should
                      be immediately zoned off to avoid anyone being exposed to the acid
                      spray or stream, and applicable valves adjusted to isolate the system and
                      stop further leakage.
                      The contaminated area should be thoroughly flushed down with copious
                      quantities of water and soda ash or lime spread around to neutralize any
                      remaining acidity.

                      If water is not available, the contaminated area should be covered with
                      sand, ashes, or gravel and acidity neutralized with soda ash or lime.

                      NEVER USE FLAMMABLE MATERIALS, such as cloth, paper, sawdust
                      or other organics, to absorb acid spills.

                      Sulphuric acid leaks, spills, or drainings must not come in contact with
                      any sulphide wastes, such as in sewers, because of the danger of evolv-
                      ing hydrogen sulphide gas.

1.8.9.5.2 First Aid Measures
                      Speed in removing sulphuric acid is of primary importance in first aid. It is
                      important to remove the patient from a contaminated area as soon as
                      possible. Medical attention should be obtained as soon as possible after
                      injury, even if the injury appears slight. The physician should be given a
                      detailed account of the incident.

                      Contact with skin and mucous membrane: Immediate removal by the use
                      of large amounts of water is urgent. If the skin contact is extensive and an
                      emergency shower is available, the employee should get under the show-
                      er immediately. Clothes can be removed while under the shower. All
                      clothing must be removed, including shoes and socks. Do not attempt to
                      neutralize the acid with chemicals.

                      In other instances, flushing with large amounts of running water, together
                      with soap and water washing, should be continued for at least fifteen min-
                      utes. Subsequent medical treatment is the same as for thermal burns.

                      Contact with eyes: If even small amounts of sulphuric acid enter the eyes,
                      they should be irrigated immediately with large amounts of water for a
                      minimum of fifteen minutes. This can be done with an eye bath, if one is
                      available, or by a gentle stream of water from a hose, or simply by pouring
                      water from any clean containers. The eyelids should be held apart during
                      irrigation to insure contact of water with all of the tissues of the surface of
                      the eyes and lids. Do not attempt to neutralize the acid with chemicals.

                      Eye irrigation should be followed with prompt medical treatment by a phy-
                      sician, preferably an eye specialist.

                      Inhalation:

                      • Remove from contaminated atmosphere.
                      • If breathing has ceased, start mouth-to-mouth artificial respiration. Ox-
                        ygen, if available, should only be administered by an experienced per-
                        son. Keep patient warm and comfortable.
                      • Taken internally: Do NOT induce vomiting. Immediately give large
                        quantities of water or milk, if available. If vomiting does occur, give flu-
                        ids again. Never give anything by mouth to an unconscious person.
                        Call a physician or the nearest Poison Control Centre immediately.

1.8.9.6    Hydrochloric Acid
                      There are two qualities of hydrochloric acid used within the chlorine plant:

                      • Hydrochloric acid is also produced and stored within the chlorine plant
                        in the hydrochloric acid synthesis unit by burning hydrogen gas and
                        chlorine gas and by absorbing the resultant hydrochloric acid vapours
                        in demineralised water. The solution contains 32% w/w hydrochloric
                        acid.
                        The 32% w/w hydrochloric acid solution is diluted to 16% w/w and used
                        within the B.L. of the chlorine plant. Please refer to Units 370 /380,
                        chapter 17, HCl Synthesis.
                      • Contaminated hydrochloric acid is received from B.L. (EDC/VCM
                        Plant) as a 15-20% solution. This solution is added to the sludge treat-
                        ment tanks in the Waste Water Treatment Unit. Please refer to
                        Unit 360, chapter 16, Waste Water Treatment.



1.8.9.6.1 Hazards
                      Hydrochloric acid is a highly corrosive and hazardous chemical and
                      should be handled with extreme care. Personnel should be properly
                      trained in the handling of hydrochloric acid and should always wear the
                      proper protective equipment when working around hydrochloric acid.

                      Hydrochloric acid is very corrosive to the skin and mucous membranes
                      and can cause severe burns to any part of the body. The eyes are espe-
                      cially sensitive to hydrochloric acid and exposure to it or its vapours im-
                      mediately causes severe irritation. If the eyes are not quickly rinsed
                      thoroughly with water, partial visual impairment or total loss of sight may
                      occur.

                      Hydrochloric acid does have excellent warning properties. Even in small
                      concentrations, hydrochloric acid vapours are easily detected. Concen-
                      trations of one to five parts per million can be detected by smell, and at
                      five to ten parts per million the smell will become disagreeable. For the
                      vapours of hydrochloric acid, hydrogen chloride, OSHA has set a ceiling
                      value of five parts per million. This means that an employee's exposure
                      to hydrogen chloride should at no time exceed five parts per million.

1.8.9.6.2 Safe Handling
                      Hydrochloric acid - both in liquid and vapour form - is a highly corrosive
                      substance that must be handled with appropriate caution.

                      Safety Equipment and Precautions

                      • Ventilation
                        Ventilation must be adequate to maintain the atmospheric concentra-
                        tion of vapour at a level not exceeding 5 ppm at any time. A National
                        Institute for Occupational Safety and Health approved acid gas car-
                        tridge respirator should be carried at all times when in areas where hy-
                        drochloric acid is handled or used.
                      • Safety Showers and Eye-Wash Fountains
                        Readily accessible, well-marked, frequently inspected safety showers
                        and eye-wash fountains should be available in areas where HCl is han-
                        dled. Showers should be capable of supplying large quantities of tem-
                        pered water. The equipment should be tested at frequent intervals.


                      Protective Equipment
                      The types of personal protective equipment needed for handling hydro-
                      chloric acid may vary. Depending on the particular operating conditions
                      involved, any or all of the following may be appropriate:

                      • Respiratory Protective Devices
                        A respirator (acid-gas cartridge) should be carried on each person at
                        all times when in areas where HCl is used. It should be used for escape
                        purposes only. Proper full-face respiratory equipment should be avail-
                        able for emergencies. This may include a positive-pressure self-con-
                        tained breathing apparatus with air. A minimum of two of these units
                        should be available at all times. The equipment should have no alumin-
                        ium parts.
                      • Protective Clothing
                        In areas of high-exposure risk, acid-impervious gloves, boots, jackets,
                        pants, and aprons should be available. Protective clothing should be
                        kept in good condition and washed to remove any hydrochloric acid
                        contamination. For normal operations, outer clothing of acid-resisting
                        fabrics is recommended. some fabrics such as nylon are unacceptable
                        because they are not acid-resistant.

                      • Eye Protection
                        Carefully fitted chemical worker’s safety goggles equipped with im-
                        pact-resistant glass or plastic lenses should always be worn whenever
                        there is danger of hydrochloric acid liquid or vapours coming in contact
                        with the eyes.
                        Plastic full-face shields eight inches or more in length with forehead
                        protection may be worn for additional protection. Chemical worker’s
                        safety goggles should be worn under the face shield.
                        Such goggles should always be worn because there is danger that
                        acid will strike the eyes from underneath or around the edge of the face
                        shield.



1.8.9.6.3 First Aid Measures
                      All employees handling hydrochloric acid should be carefully instructed in
                      first aid procedures, and these procedures should be reviewed regularly.

                      • Eye Contact
                        Eye contact with HCl (liquid or vapours) will cause irritation and may
                        cause severe burns. Impairment of vision or even total loss of sight
                        may occur. Irrigate exposed eyes immediately with large quantities of
                        running water for at least 30 minutes. Notify an ophthalmologist imme-
                        diately. Make sure hands are free of HCl contamination, then use
                        hands to hold eyelids apart to ensure contact of water with all accessi-
                        ble tissues of the eyes and lids.
                      • Skin Contact
                        HCl has a corrosive action on the skin and mucous membranes that
                        may cause severe burns. Flood affected area immediately with large
                        amounts of water. Remove clothing immediately while in shower and
                        notify a doctor. If eyes are not affected, do not remove safety goggles
                        until head has been rinsed for 15 minutes. Washing should continue
                        for at least 30 minutes. Do not attempt to neutralise the hydrogen chlo-
                        ride with alkaline solutions.
                      • Inhalation
                        Inhalation of HCl immediately produces severe irritation of the upper
                        respiratory tract, resulting in coughing, burning of the throat and chok-
                        ing sensations. Occasionally, ulceration of the throat and larynx or
                        edema of the lungs has resulted. HCl vapours are very irritating, thus
                        giving ample warning of the presence of dangerous concentrations.

                          should be given only upon advice of qualified medical personnel.
                      • Ingestion
                        When concentrated hydrochloric acid is swallowed it causes severe
                        burning of the mucous membranes of the mouth, oesophagus, and
                        stomach.
                        Conscious persons who have swallowed hydrochloric acid should be
                        given large amounts of water, or milk if available. Transport immediate-
                        ly to a medical facility. Do not induce vomiting. Do not give anything by
                        mouth an unconscious victim.

1.9        PRECOMMISSIONING AND COMMISSIONING

1.9.1      GENERAL

1.9.1.1    General Exposure
                      Commissioning activities take place after Mechanical Completion of the
                      systems has been accomplished and before the start-up of the plant.

                      Commissioning is primarily a dynamic/functional verification of equip-
                      ment and facilities which are grouped in operational systems or part of
                      systems.

                      Commissioning activities shall ensure by testing and inspection that facil-
                      ities can be started up and operated safely and efficiently within its design
                      limits.

                      The verifications should be carried out and documented in a uniform way
                      as recommended in this manual and the respective procedures and work
                      instructions.

1.9.2      PRECOMMISSIONING, GENERAL INSTRUCTIONS
                      Following activities are established as part of precommissioning and will
                      be performed by erection personnel as part of the Mechanical Completion
                      (MC) activities:

                      • Inspection of plant completeness
                      • Pressure testing
                      • Cleaning of the plant sections
                      • Draining of the plant sections
                      • Drying with air and preservation of plant sections
                      • Charging of lubricants
                      • Checking of seals and packings
                      • Cold alignment of rotating equipment
                      • Inspection of electrical equipment and installation
                      • Inspection of instrumentation installation
                      • Reinstallation of the plant sections
                      • Testing and installation of pressure relief devices
                      • Internal inspection of equipment
                      • House keeping
                      • Installation of final piping gaskets
                      • Checking of availability of chemicals and utilities handled
                      • Pickling, Chemical Cleaning

1.9.2.1    Inspection of the Plant for Completeness
                      The plant is inspected visually for completeness and correct execution of
                      construction work according to the documentation.

                      From a strictly technical and mechanical point of view, the following items
                      have to be checked principally:

                      1. Correct connection and tie-in of process vessels, machinery and pip-
                         ing.
                      2. Installation of valves (control valves, check valves, etc.) in the cor-
                         rect direction of flow.
                      3. Sufficient number of line vents and drains.
                      4. Accessibility of valves.
                      5. Correct installation of safety valves and correct set pressure on
                         safety valve tag plate.
                      6. On-spec insulation.
                      7. Threshold limit values and functions of safety trips, if this check is
                         not deferred until commissioning.
                      8. Use of the specified material for piping, valves, flanges, thermowells,
                         bolts, etc. If in doubt, a non-destructive test is to be performed.
                      9. Proper pre-stressing of piping spring hangers and compensators.
                      10. Proper execution of fixed and sliding points.

                          forces acting on them (e. g. blow-off lines of safety valves).
                      12. Orientation and bearing clearance of machinery taking into account
                          the expected expansion at max. allowable working temperature.

                      14. Blind flanges, screens, strainers and spades installed during erec-
                          tion for flushing or pressurising are to be listed and also shown in the
                          documents.
                      15. Temporary branches and connection used during erection have to
                          be removed.
                      16. Process vessels and columns

1.9.2.2    Pressure Testing
                      New or repaired plant sections and pipelines are subject to a hydraulic
                      test as part of the Mechanical Completion.

                      The hydrostatic pressure test is carried out by the ERECTION personnel.

                      The following general instruction is only an information for the precom-
                      missioning and commissioning personnel to understand the procedure of
                      pressure testing.

                      Note:       This is no instruction for ERECTION personnel!

                      • The test pressure applied shall be fixed by the team responsible for
                        ERECTION under consideration of design pressure of piping and
                        equipment and Iranian regulations and engineering specs. etc. for
                        pressure testing.
                      • Conduct the pressure test without pumps, instrumentation equipment.
                        Equipment has to be blinded or removed and replaced by spool piec-
                        es.

                                                          Doc. ID-Code                          Rev.
Copyright 2005 Uhde GmbH
                                                    8408205-CB-PR-MNL-0102                       02

                      • All systems to be tested are to be closed against other plant sections
                        by blind flanges. A closed valve only is not sufficient.
                      • Prior to the pressure test, safety valves should be removed.
                      • At first, the section to be tested is put under low excess pressure in or-
                        der to find out major leakage.
                      • These leakages must be eliminated after depressurising the section.
                        After the required repair work, the relevant parts must be thoroughly
                        cleaned before assembly.
                      • Leakage which cannot be eliminated by careful tightening of bolts must
                        be clearly marked.
                      • Leakage at stuffing boxes of gate and globe valves can be repaired in
                        the first step by tightening of the stuffing box gland. Take care not to
                        tighten the stuffing box too hard since then rotation of the spindle may
                        become difficult. Very untight stuffing boxes must get a new packing.
                      • If no leakage can be found immediately, the section should be held un-
                        der pressure for a certain period. Sealing is satisfactory when pressure
                        decrease is within the limits fixed by the team responsible for EREC-
                        TION.
                      • Conduct all operational leak tests after assembly of all equipment dur-
                        ing the commissioning.

1.9.2.2.1 Hydrostatic Testing
                      If liquids are used for the pressure test, it must be checked whether:

                      • the allowable foundation load of apparatus and vessels is not exceed-
                        ed,
                      • the pipes of large diameter are sufficiently supported,
                      • the systems can be vented at all necessary points,
                      • the plant can be completely drained.
                      If water is used for pressure testing, flushing, cleaning or leak testing, the
                      water shall be free of dirt, iron oxides and organic substances. Water con-
                      taining chloride ions might cause pitting and stress corrosion on austenit-
                      ic CrNi steel, nickel and nickel alloys if the chloride ions reach a critical
                      concentration (e.g. in a water droplet remaining in the system after test-
                      ing). An increase in temperature will accelerate the corrosion rate. Once
                      present, chloride ions are very difficult to remove even by subsequent
                      flushing with de-mineralized water.

                      The quality of the water shall be evidenced by an analysis prior to use. If
                      the same water is used several times, interim analysis shall be made.

                      The testing agents to be used for pressure testing are given in ANNEX
                      A28, FLUIDLIST WITH DEFINITION FOR DEGREE OF CLEANLINESS.

1.9.2.2.2 Pneumatic Testing
                      Pneumatic testing is potentially a more dangerous operation than hydro-
                      static testing. At the pressure ranges most frequently encountered the
                      amount of energy containing in air under pressure is more than 200 times
                      the energy containing in water at the same pressure and volume. Pneu-
                      matic testing is recommended, where drying is hardly to achieve and re-
                      maining water disturbs the process, e.g. refrigeration circuits.

                      If gases are used for pressure test, it must be ensured that:

                      • the Iranian regulation for pneumatic testing and common engineering
                        practice of pneumatic testing are observed.
                      • the test gas pressure for apparatus and vessels is to be defined in re-
                        spect of the design pressure and the Iranian regulation for pneumatic
                        testing.
                      • the site shall be clear of personnel not directly associated with the test
                        (e.g. perform the test out of normal working hours).
                      • personnel barricades shall be erected at a defined distance to the test-
                        ed equipment (distance accord. Iranian regulation for pneumatic test-
                        ing).
                      • it has to be considered that if the testing equipment should fail during
                        pneumatic pressure testing, other equipment in the vicinity may be
                        damaged.
                      • the compressor utilised for feeding the medium is suitable at the re-
                        quired pressures.

                      Please also refer to ANNEX A28, FLUIDLIST WITH DEFINITION FOR
                      DEGREE OF CLEANLINESS.

                      The following general instruction should be followed:

                      • Blowing or flushing shall be performed section by section to ensure
                        equally high velocity of the fluid over the whole section to be cleaned.
                        Velocity may only be reduced at the point of supply.
                      • The flushing flow rate should be higher than the later operating flow
                        rate. In order to increase the quantity of flushing agent, upstream
                        equipment may be used as buffers. However, the mechanical load act-
                        ing on the equipment during flushing shall not exceed the design loads.
                      • Cleaning shall preferably be performed in the operational flow direc-
                        tion. Orifice plates, control valves, steam traps etc. are to be removed.
                        Connections to machinery are to be shut off. Discharge valves shall ei-
                        ther be dismounted or at least opened widely.
                      • Process vessels with loose internals and equipment already filled with
                        packing material may only be flushed at velocity equivalent to the later
                        operating load. The flushing fluid is to be selected carefully to avoid
                        damage to the equipment (e. g. avoid exceeding the relevant design
                        temperature).
                      • Care shall be taken to avoid that removed contaminants are entrained
                        to equipment items, where they can settle. To prevent this the lines up-
                        stream such equipment are to be cleaned first via suitable branches.
                      • Process vessels and piping designed for low maximum allowable
                        working temperatures, which are to be cleaned by steam, shall be
                        checked for possible expansion prior to flushing. Drain valves shall
                        only be used as outlet for the flushing agent if they have roughly the
                        same diameter as the pipeline.
                      • To flush a unit with the process fluid, first the main supply line is to be
                        either flushed at one go or section by section. Then the main supply
                        line is pressurised and the piping branching off from it is cleaned con-
                        secutively up to the connections to the supply points or consumers. All
                        connections and instruments are to be blown out or flushed also.
                      • Each individual train of pipes is to be flushed until the flushing agent
                        leaving it is clean. Some utilities systems can be sufficiently cleaned
                        using their respective process fluid. Steam piping is cleaned by steam,
                        instrument air lines by air or compressed air and nitrogen piping with
                        nitrogen. Alloyed piping is to be flushed with demineralised water.
                        Flushing media have to fulfil the same criteria as the media used for
                        hydrostatic pressure test. After flushing, the liquid is to be drained en-

                          suring that no negative pressure builds up. Sufficient venting is to be
                          ensured when draining liquid from process equipment and vessels.
                      • Equipment and piping networks which have to be flushed with liquid
                        agents are to be blown dry or filled with process fluid afterwards. After
                        cleaning, the clean unit is to be made ready for operation. Orifice
                        plates, control valves, strainers, etc. are to be installed and the instru-
                        ment connections are to be made ready for operation. Blinds and aux-
                        iliary piping are to be removed and auxiliary connections are to be

                        runs.
                      • A header or a utility distribution system is cleaned in a way that at first
                        the main supply line is flushed completely or in sections. After that, the
                        main line is pressurised and branches are cleaned one after the other
                        up to the connections at the supply points to the consumers. All con-

1.9.2.4    Draining and Drying of Plant Sections
                      After the flushing of process lines, the water is drained from the system.

                      During the water drainage or during the time the liquid level in a tank or
                      apparatus is being lowered, care should be taken that adequate air can
                      be drawn in order to avoid the formation of a vacuum.

                      After draining the liquid a purging with air should follow.

                      Where the drying and inertisation of plant section is necessary, the
                      flushed sections should be first purged with air and than purged with ni-
                      trogen.

                      For details please refer to the Work Instruction "Nitrogen Purging" and
                      "Steam flushing" (see ANNEX A15, WORK INSTRUCTIONS).

1.9.2.8    Reinstallation
                      After the cleaning respectively pickling is completed, it should be carefully
                      checked whether all temporary connections have been removed and all
                      temporary removed parts have been reinstalled.



1.9.2.9    Testing and Installation of Pressure Relief Devices
                      Careful handling of safety/relief valves in transit is important. Rough han-
                      dling can change the pressure setting or deform relief valve parts so that
                      they will not operate properly. Relief valves should be treated as delicate
                      instruments. Before installation, it is recommended to test all safety/relief
                      valves at site to check that the set pressure is correct and the valve is in
                      good working order.
                      Minimum requirement is to test at least the safety relief valves with dam-
                      aged seals or missing certificate and seal them again.
                      This should be done according manufacturer's specification and Iranian
                      regulation.
                      The OWNER'S personnel shall ensure that this is done and that test cer-
                      tificates are valid.



1.9.2.10   Internal Inspection of Equipment
                      Before final closing of vessels and reactors, the checking of the internals
                      is important with regard to completeness and cleanliness.
                      Furthermore, the correct connections and material of all pipes, correct in-
                      stallation of all measuring nozzles, reference vessels for level control,
                      drains, etc. has to be checked.
                      Results and details of internal inspection of equipment shall be collected
                      in the commissioning dossiers of the respective unit/system.

                      Note:       Inspection should be scheduled before blanketing the equip-
                                  ment with nitrogen.

           Plant
                      In the fluidlist the need of pickling is defined by the degree of

1.9.2.11.2 General Instructions for Pickling
                      • All measuring devices have to be dismantled and replaced by spool pi-
                        eces if necessary.
                      • All control valves have to be dismantled and replaced by spool pieces.
                      • Pickling cycles systems have to be separated from other parts of the
                        systems by spectacle blinds.
                      • When using hydrochloric acid as pickling agent, care has to be taken
                        that stainless steel is not brought in contact with it. All equipment using
                        stainless steel as material of construction has to be dismantled, to be
                        bypassed or to be replaced by spool pieces.
                      • Before starting chemical treatment, the volume (hold up) of each pick-
                        ling cycle has to be defined.
                      • Systems which are already pickled have to be inertised. Any later ad-
                        mission of atmosphere has to be avoided at any circumstances. If sec-
                        tions are inertised with nitrogen special safety measures have to be
                        taken.

1.9.2.11.3 Instructions for the Pickling of Process Lines
                      The pickling procedure for process lines in the C/A Plant (if necessary)
                      consists of the following steps:

                      1. Degreasing with 1 % sodium hydroxide solution, Duration: approx. 2
                         hours, 80 - 90°C.
                      2. Draining and flushing with water.
                      3. Pickling for derusting with 5 - 7 % hydrochloric acid containing a cor-
                         rosion inhibitor (for example HAG 0.1 - 0.2 % Recline 213) or an
                         other suitable acid pickling agent. Duration: approx. 4-6 hours, 60°C.
                      4. Draining and flushing with water containing 0.1 % citric acid (passi-
                         vation).
                      5. Draining and flushing with 1 % sodium hydroxide solution for neutral-
                         isation.
                      6. Draining and flushing with demineralized water.


                      Opening all drain points and dead ends, purging and drying with air.

                      With permission of the representative of OWNER piping lines can be
                      pressurised with nitrogen for preservation. If this is not possible adequate
                      preservative has to be used.

                      Note:       The pickling process has to be monitored analytically under all
                                  circumstances. Log sheets should be used.

1.9.2.11.4 Instructions for Degreasing of Process Lines in the C/A Plant
                      Degreasing is defined by the degree of cleanliness 6, please refer to
                      chapter 1.9.2.3. - Cleaning of the Plant Sections.

                      Degreasing of piping and equipment means, that when such piping and
                      equipment is placed in service it must be free of oil, grease or any organic
                      contaminants and loose particles that may come in contact with the fluid.

                      Please refer to FLUIDLIST in ANNEX A28.

1.9.2.11.5 General Instructions for Degreasing
                      • All measuring devices have to be dismantled and replaced by spool pi-

                      • All control valves have to be dismantled and replaced by spool pieces.
                      • Control valves have to be degreased separately or the valves have to

                        taken.


1.9.2.11.6 Instructions for the Degreasing of Process Lines
                      The degreasing procedure for process lines in the C/A Plant (if neces-
                      sary) consists of the following steps:

                      1. Flushing with water.
                      2. Degreasing with 1 % sodium hydroxide solution, Duration: approx. 2
                         hours, 80 - 90°C.
                      3. Draining and flushing with water.
                      4. Draining and flushing with water containing 0.1 % citric acid (passi-
                         vation).
                      5. Draining and flushing with water.
                      6. Purging with air, opening all drain points and dead ends.
                      7. Drying and purging with nitrogen.

                      For dry chlorine piping please also refer to chapter 1.9.3.1.

1.9.3      PRECOMMISSIONING, SPECIAL INSTRUCTIONS (C/A PLANT)
                      The chlorine plant requires some very specific precommissioning activi-
                      ties for safe commissioning and start-up:

                      For cleaning, pressure and leak testing please also refer to ANNEX A28,
                      FLUIDLIST WITH DEFINITION FOR DEGREE OF CLEANLINESS.

1.9.3.1    Dry Chlorine Gas Piping
                      All piping, instrumentation and equipment handling dry chlorine must be
                      pressure tested cleaned, de-greased and dried.

                      Recommendations for dry chlorine gas piping preparation:

                      • Cleaning
                        All portions of new chlorine systems must be cleaned before use, be-
                        cause chlorine can react violently with cutting oil, grease, and other for-
                        eign materials. Cleaning must not be done with hydrocarbons or
                        alcohols, because residual solvent may react with chlorine. Any equip-
                        ment received in an oily condition should be dismantled and cleaned
                        before use.
                        Three methods are used to clean piping systems. These are water
                        washing / steam cleaning, sand-blasting, and solvent cleaning. Some-
                        times, a combination of methods is most useful in a given situation.
                             • Water Washing / Steam Cleaning
                               This method is useful for both new construction and plant mainte-
                               nance. Care must be taken to ensure that the system is properly
                               dried after cleaning. Particular attention must be paid to joint areas
                               where water could collect. It is common to change all gaskets after
                               water washing.



                                                            Doc. ID-Code                          Rev.
Copyright 2005 Uhde GmbH
                                                      8408205-CB-PR-MNL-0102                       02
                                            PVC Arvand
                                          Operating Manual
                                                                         National Petrochemical comany
                 SAZE H
                 C O NSU LTANTS                C/A Plant                 Arvand Petrochemical
                                                                              Company
Uhde Project No: 03-3039             Sazeh Project No: 8047           Owner Project No: 8408205
Job Code:        PVC Arvand          Job Code:                        Owner Job Code: PVC Arvand
                                                                                        Page 125 of 967


                             • Sand-Blast Cleaning
                               This method is used primarily on large piping sections for new con-
                               struction. Care must be taken to isolate valves, instruments, and
                               process equipment form potential damage. All residual sand must
                               be removed from pipe sections prior to installation. If care is taken
                               to exclude moisture, the assembled system will be ready for dry air
                               or nitrogen drying.
                             • Solvent Cleaning
                               This method is used when a system cannot tolerate water or is not
                               suitable for sand-blast cleaning. Also, it is used for individual
                               valves, relief valves, and instruments. Many solvents are excellent
                               cleaning agents but pose significant risks due to toxicity or flamma-
                               bility. The best overall solvent must be available as a liquid in con-
                               venient containers, be nearly non reactive with chlorine, be
                               nonflammable, have relatively low vapour pressure and a low tox-
                               icity rating, and be a good cleaning solvent at reasonable cost. The
                               recommend solvent is 1,1,1 trichloroethane, which meets the cri-
                               teria above. Also trichloro-trifluoroethane has suitable physical
                               properties, although it is available only in cylinders or ton contain-
                               ers at higher cost. Because of toxicity and health hazard, carbon
                               tetrachloride, chloroform, trichloroethylene, methylene chloride,
                               and other such solvents are not recommended. Any solvent usage
                               requires personnel safeguards, good work practices, suitable col-
                               lection, and safe and environmentally acceptable disposal of resid-
                               ual materials.
                      • Hydrostatic Testing
                        New or rewelded chlorine piping should be hydrostatical tested to 1.5
                        times the maximum pressure to which the system may be subjected.
                        Pressure gauges, relief valves, automatic control valves, and other
                        components which may be damaged should be removed and openings
                        should be blocked off prior to testing. After testing, all moisture-absorb-
                        ing gaskets and valve packings should be replaced. It is essential that
                        chlorine systems be thoroughly dried prior to being put into service.
                        There are some circumstances under which drying cannot be accom-
                        plished after hydrostatic testing with water. If drying is impractical and
                        the equipment and components comply in all other respects with the
                        provisions of this pamphlet, hydrostatic testing may be omitted and the
                        equipment thoroughly cleaned, leak-tested, and prepared for service
                        as applicable.
                      • Drying


                                                            Doc. ID-Code                          Rev.
Copyright 2005 Uhde GmbH
                                                      8408205-CB-PR-MNL-0102                       02
                                          PVC Arvand
                                        Operating Manual
                                                                        National Petrochemical comany
                 SAZE H
                 C O NSU LTANTS               C/A Plant                 Arvand Petrochemical
                                                                             Company
Uhde Project No: 03-3039            Sazeh Project No: 8047           Owner Project No: 8408205
Job Code:        PVC Arvand         Job Code:                        Owner Job Code: PVC Arvand
                                                                                       Page 126 of 967


                          Chlorine piping systems must always be dried before being placed in
                          service. Even if water has not been purposely introduced into the sys-
                          tem for hydrostatic testing or cleaning, drying still is required because
                          moisture may enter the system from the atmosphere or other sources.
                          Where steam has been used for cleaning, the steaming can be fol-
                          lowed directly by the introduction of nitrogen or dry air, at a dew point
                          of -40°C or below, blown through the line until the existing gas has a -
                          40°C or lower dew point.
                          Direct drying using ambient-temperature dry air or nitrogen purge may
                          take an extended period of time. Consideration can be given to using
                          the services of commercial system dehydrators, which dry piping and
                          equipment by circulating or purging with large volumes of heated nitro-
                          gen or other dry inert gas.
                          It is also possible to use the chlorine compressor to stack air through
                          the drying towers (already commissioned with 98% H2SO4). The dry
                          air can be used to dry the chlorine system unit the resident moisture
                          content is less 20 ppm w/w (see chapter 1.9.5.2.6).
                      • Valves
                        Valves require special attention. Most valves, regardless of style, have
                        pockets where water can be trapped, especially if the valve is fully
                        open. Valves left in the piping system must be fixed in the half-open
                        position when the system is being dried. Valves removed temporarily
                        from the system during the drying operation also must be checked to
                        ensure that water or moisture is not trapped in a cavity. These valves
                        must be dried thoroughly prior to replacement in the piping system if
                        they are not dried with the rest of the system. Personnel responsible
                        for drying the system should be familiar with valve construction and be
                        aware of places where water or moisture can be trapped.
                      • Testing for Leaks
                        After drying, the system should be leak-tested by pressuring to
                        0,4 barg with dry air or nitrogen. Use soap solution to test for leaks at
                        joints.

                          When detectable leaks have been repaired, the line should be re-test-
                          ed. Any effort to detect the source of a leak should be carried out with
                          full consideration for potential hazards. Appropriate protective equip-
                          ment must be used.

1.9.3.3    Washing, Filling and Flushing of Antracite
                      Wasting, filling and flushing of anthracite is used for its absorbent capac-
                      ity and its capability to remove dissolved organics, as filter medium in the
                      filters 41FT05101A-J (41FT05201A-J).

                      Anthracite is to be washed before filling into the filters.

                      • Filling of Antracite
                             • For this purpose anthracite as received in various sizes 2-4 mm
                               and 1.4 - 2.5 mm are washed thoroughly with process water and
                               any foreign materials present are removed.
                             • 0.6 - 1.6 mm size can be filled directly in the filter and can be
                               washed with raw water.

                                  Caution:
                                  Charging of anthracite to filter is to be done carefully taking care
                                  that filling is done with correct quantity of each size grade of an-
                                  thracite. Anthracite should not be dropped from top of the filter
                                  since this can crumble the anthracite. It should be unloaded man-
                                  ually inside the filter from a container and care has to be taken not
                                  to damage the filter nozzles. For safety fill the filters with raw water
                                  before filling anthracite.

                             • While filling, the highest size range is filled at the bottom and small-
                               est at the top. The button layers act as support grade.
                             • The bottom most bed should cover the collecting nozzles.

1.9.3.7    Caustic Evaporation Unit
                      The Caustic Evaporation Unit is a integrated Package Unit supplied by
                      Bertrams Chemical Plants LTD. For pre-commissioning information
                      please refer also to vendor documentation of Requisition 840-CB-PU-
                      REQ-0006.

                      Special attention to be paid to:

                      • Vacuum and Condensate System
                        Inspection of the vacuum system of the falling film evaporators 41E-
                        32051 and 41E-32052 for leakage. It is only possible to proceed with
                        the pre-commissioning, if the lower part of the falling evaporators and
                        the vapour condensate tank 41V-32051 are filled with demin water in
                        order to secure barometric connection.
                             • Falling Film Evaporators 41E-32051 and 41E-32052
                               Unfortunately the vacuum test cannot be done at operating vacu-
                               um, because the water is sucked up much higher than the caustic
                               (different density), thus the vacuum at the falling film evaporator
                               would be broken. This fact, however, is not important for the vac-
                               uum test because, for example already at 550 mbar, relevant infor-
                               mation on tightness can be obtained. Therefore, the vacuum pump
                               will be stopped after having achieved this value.
                               The pressure increase in this system should not exceed 133 mbar/
                               h. If this is not the case, all flanged connections must be checked
                               for leaks.
                             • Steam condensate tank system and vacuum condensate tank sys-
                               tem must be checked, cleaned and flushed with demin water.
                      • Falling Film Evaporators
                        In principle, the inside of the falling film evaporators 41E-32051, 41E-
                        32052 and 41E-32053 does not require an inspection, but it is neces-
                        sary to check that the slotted in-feed devices fit perfectly onto the
                        tubes. For this inspection it is required to remove the top cover of the
                        falling film evaporator. After the inspection, the falling film evaporator
                        must be washed out very carefully with soft water through the steam
                        flushing nozzle.

1.9.4       COMMISSIONING, GENERAL INSTRUCTIONS
                      A successful start-up of a plant depends on the thorough performance of
                      precommissioning, commissioning and the perfect supply of utilities, test-
                      ing, flushing- and dry-out agents as well as feed stocks and chemicals.

                      After checking plant for completeness, correct execution of precommis-
                      sioning and commissioning the plant should be ready for operation and
                      feed stocks can be introduced to commence the process operation and
                      start up the plant.

                      Following activities are established as part of commissioning and will be
                      performed by the OWNER under CONTRACTORS/ PROCESS OWN-
                      ERS supervision:

                      • Checking of installations against P&IDs
                      • Checking of cleanliness
                      • Inspection of critical equipment
                      • Livening of utility system
                      • Leak testing
                      • Blanketing with nitrogen
                      • Charging of chemicals
                      • Function Test of electrical equipment and installation
                      • Function Test of instrumentation equipment and installation
                      • Hot alignment and function test of rotating equipment
                      • Checking of supports for hot settings
                      • Labelling of pipelines and equipment

1.9.4.2    General Commissioning Instructions
                      All commissioning activities of the C/A Plant shall be scheduled and doc-
                      umented and in the proposed Commissioning Dossiers
                      (see chapter 1.91.6).

1.9.4.2.1 Checking of installation against P&ID’s
                      The plant is inspected visually for completeness and correct execution of
                      construction work according to the P&ID’s.

                      The following summary indicates the most important points to be checked
                      from the point of view of process or operation:

                      • Correct direction of flow through check valves and control valves;
                      • High or low points in the piping layout where troubles may occur during
                        operation.
                      • Correct installation of instruments, alarm devices and electric equip-
                        ment.
                      • Accessibility and operability of valves.
                      • Sufficient number of high-point vents and low-point drains.
                      • Proper installation of the safety valves connections.
                      • Correct set pressure of safety valves and rupture disk tag plate.
                      • Correct connection at the beginning and at the end of each line; correct
                        location and design of pipe routing.
                      For the documentation of the PID check a set of marked PID and a check/
                      punch list is recommended.

1.9.4.2.2 Checking of Cleanliness
                      During precommissioning, all plant sections and piping systems including
                      the utility system must be thoroughly cleaned from impurities such as
                      scales, sand, welding pearls, etc.

                      Because the cleaning has been performed during precommissioning by
                      erection personnel following the general instructions given in chapter
                      "Cleaning of the plant sections" only spot checks are necessary.

1.9.4.4.1 General - Testing of Instrument Loops
                      Definitions:

                      • FCS:         Field Control System
                      • CCR:         Central Control Room
                      • FTC:         Field Termination Cabinets
                      • MCC:         Motor Control Centre
                      • LIR:         Local Instrument Room
                      • SCD:         System Control Diagram
                      • C&E:         Cause and Effect Diagram
                      • VDU:         Visual Display Unit (FCS operator station)
                      • ESD:         Emergency Shutdown System


                      The loop test shall ensure that all components in a loop are fully opera-
                      tional when connected together and in a state ready for multi discipline
                      commissioning.

                      The complete instrument loop shall be tested as one system. If a field de-
                      vice is not correctly calibrated a re-calibration shall be carried out.

                      Checking of set point for alarms, trips, control functions and displays on
                      VDU's are included in the loop test.

                      Prior to start of a loop test, it shall be ensured that all necessary docu-
                      mentation in the correct revision are available, that the field installation is
                      mechanical complete and the FCS / ESD is prepared for loop test. This
                      includes power up of FCS / ESD units.

                      MCC power, instrument air and hydraulic power shall be provided. The
                      permanent headers shall be used. If temporary systems are necessary,
                      they shall be sufficient to give a realistic test of equipment (valve) per-
                      formance.

                      Level 1 loop test
                      This is considered as a part of a loop test only (temporary powered when
                      the FCS / ESD is not available). This level will only be accepted when it
                      is impossible to do a level 3 loop test. An example is a check on a supplier
                      skid before delivery.



                      Level 3 loop test

                      This is a complete loop test, covering all the devices and information
                      shown on the loop drawing, and all control and monitoring functions relat-
                      ed to a loop drawing presented on VDU's and graphics.

                      The test includes all field devices. When checking the functionality of the
                      loop, the field devices, power distribution, input and output modules and
                      hardware and software modules in FCS shall be used. All kinds of display
                      functions on Operator stations shall be checked. This shall include ad-
                      dressing/reading/presentation of values and status related to all input/
                      output shown on loop drawing. Correct implementation in FCS of control
                      logic as defined on system control diagrams and interlock descriptions /
                      Cause and Effect lists shall be checked to the extent possible.

                      Permanent instrument air distribution and MCC power systems shall be
                      used to the extent possible.



                      Loop Drawings, Short Description

                      The Instrument loop drawing shows the termination of any field device
                      linked up against "systems" in CCR (FCS,ESD,PLC`s etc.). It can be one
                      or multiple field devices on one loop drawing.

                      The loop drawing also includes interfaces to the Motor Control Centre.
                      References to software blocks, representation on graphics and other dis-
                      plays and interlock diagrams etc. have to be taken from System vendor´s
                      documentation.

1.9.4.4.2 Loop Test Execution
                      The Instrument Loop Drawing, System Control Diagrams (SCD), Inter-
                      locking descriptions, Cause & Effect Diagrams and in same cases, Ven-
                      dor logic specifications define the extent of test necessary for each loop.

                      Loops which cannot be tested completely, shall be tested to the extent
                      possible.

                      The extent of the tests shall be marked on the loop diagram, such that a
                      full loop test can be completed later.

                      Safety Systems
                      Special precautions will often be included in safety systems like fire de-
                      tection, gas detection and emergency shut down systems. Monitoring
                      loops of these systems will usually be provided with earth fault check,
                      check for short circuit and open circuit. When testing these loops, the test
                      shall include simulating of these faults.

                      Out of Range Test
                      Loops shall be tested for out of range conditions. Such conditions may be
                      too high and too low process input, loss of air supply, loss of electric pow-
                      er and loss of loop signals. The loop test technician shall check that the
                      loop has been designed for correct reaction on failures as per data sheet/
                      PID.

                      Loop Test and Calibration
                      When all the installation checks are completed, the loop shall be tested.

                      The loop test, and when necessary, the re-calibration shall be done,
                      when possible, in one working step.

                      In order to do the loop test, process conditions to the largest extent pos-
                      sible, shall always be simulated by the use of real physical conditions
                      (hand pumps, physical activation of switches etc.). Simulation of switches
                      by short circuit or simulation of the electrical signal from transmitters is
                      only acceptable real process conditions cannot be established by testing
                      tools (for instance Vortex or Coriolis flow transmitters).

                      If datasheets have been changed after delivery of instruments, OWNER
                      shall recalibrate the instrument.
